title: Silver That Darkens in the Sun
summary: Some chemicals made with silver turn dark when sunlight touches them. In the 1700s and early 1800s, curious scientists used this trick to make the first light-drawn shadow pictures of words, leaves and lace. But the pictures kept darkening until they turned completely black, and nobody could figure out how to make them stop.

sections.heading: A Bottle That Wrote in the Sunshine
paragraphs: Picture a university laboratory in Germany around the year 1717. Glass flasks and jars crowd the shelves, a fire crackles in a furnace, and the air smells sharply of acid. A professor named Johann Heinrich Schulze is mixing chalk with nitric acid, a strong acid that can dissolve metals. Without realizing it, he is using acid that has some silver dissolved in it. He sets the cloudy mixture down near a sunny window. When he comes back, he notices something odd. The side of the bottle facing the window has turned a deep dark red-purple, while the side facing the room is still pale.

Schulze, born in 1687, was a busy scholar who taught medicine and studied ancient languages at the universities of Altdorf and later Halle. He was the kind of person who could not leave a mystery alone. Was the darkening caused by the heat of the Sun or by its light? Plenty of chemicals change when they get warm, so heat seemed like a reasonable guess.

To find out, he did what good scientists do: he tested one thing at a time. He warmed a sample of the mixture by a fire, out of the sunlight. It did not darken. So heat alone was not the cause. Then he tried something clever and playful. He cut words and letters out of paper to make stencils, and he stuck them onto the outside of a bottle of the mixture. He placed the bottle in direct sunlight. Where light shone through the cut-out letters, the liquid darkened. Where the paper blocked the light, it stayed pale. When he peeled the stencils away, the words appeared written inside the bottle in dark letters.

It was the first time anyone had used light on purpose to make a lasting-looking pattern on a light-sensitive chemical. It was not quite a photograph, but it was something close: writing done by the Sun. Of course, it did not last. If he shook the bottle, the dark parts mixed with the pale parts and the letters disappeared. If he left the bottle in the light, the whole mixture darkened and the words vanished into the dark.

Schulze gave his light-sensitive mixture the name Scotophorus, meaning "darkness-bringer", in contrast to phosphorus, which means "light-bringer". He seems to have thought it might be useful for testing whether a mineral contained silver. He did not think of using it to make pictures. He described his experiments in a paper published in 1719. Many books give the date as 1727, but that was a reprint, and the experiments themselves were done around 1717.

Schulze was not the very first person to notice that silver compounds change in light. Back in 1614 an Italian-born chemist named Angelo Sala had noticed that powdered silver nitrate turned black in the Sun, and in 1694 the scientist Wilhelm Homberg described how light darkened certain chemicals. But Schulze was the first to prove carefully that light, and not heat, was responsible. Because of this, some German writers count him as an early inventor of photography. That is a stretch, but he certainly found one of the key ingredients.

sections.heading: A Novel, a Prism and the Color Violet
paragraphs: Before scientists worked out how to save a picture made by light, a storyteller imagined it. In 1760 a French writer named Charles-François Tiphaigne de la Roche published a strange fantasy novel called Giphantie. In it, a traveler visits a magical land where spirits have learned to coat a canvas with a sticky substance that captures the image of whatever is in front of it, like a mirror, and then dries so the picture stays forever, perfect in every detail. The author did not think of light-sensitive chemicals; he imagined the substance trapped the image because it was gooey. But he described the dream perfectly: a mirror that remembers.

Meanwhile, real science was creeping closer. Carl Wilhelm Scheele was born in 1742 in Stralsund, a town on the Baltic coast that then belonged to Sweden. At about fourteen he became an apprentice in a pharmacy, a shop where medicines were mixed by hand, and he spent much of his life working as a pharmacist in small Swedish towns, doing brilliant chemistry in his spare time. He discovered oxygen independently of other scientists, and he helped identify chlorine, barium, molybdenum and tungsten. He was elected to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in 1775.

In 1777 Scheele published a famous book on air and fire. In it he described experiments with silver chloride, a white powder that forms when silver meets chlorine. He knew it darkened in the light, and he wanted to know what was really going on. First, he looked at the dark material. He found that if he poured ammonia over the darkened powder, the unchanged white silver chloride dissolved away, but tiny black particles were left behind. Those particles were metallic silver. So light was breaking silver chloride apart, setting free specks of pure silver, which look black when they are that small.

Without knowing it, Scheele had also found a way to fix a light picture. Ammonia could wash away the silver chloride that light had not touched, leaving only the dark silver behind. If someone had put the two ideas together, photography might have arrived decades earlier. But nobody did. Early picture-makers either did not know about Scheele's result or did not realize what it meant.

Scheele's second discovery was about color. He used a glass prism, a triangular block of glass that splits sunlight into a rainbow, called a spectrum. He laid a piece of paper coated with silver chloride so that the rainbow fell across it. The paper did not darken evenly. Under the violet end of the rainbow it turned dark quickly, while under the red end it hardly changed at all. Violet light was far more powerful at causing the chemical change than red light.

Today we know why. Light comes in tiny packets of energy, and violet and blue light carry more energy per packet than red light. Only packets with enough energy can knock the silver chloride apart. This discovery had a very practical result much later. Photographers learned that they could work with light-sensitive paper and film under a dim red lamp without spoiling it. That is why old-fashioned darkrooms glow red. A few years later, in 1801, the German scientist Johann Wilhelm Ritter used the same kind of silver chloride test and found that the paper darkened even beyond the violet end of the rainbow, where the eye sees nothing. He had discovered invisible ultraviolet light. Silver, it turned out, could detect things human eyes could not.

Scheele died in 1786, at only 43. Doctors said the cause was mercury poisoning, most likely from years of handling dangerous chemicals. He never made a picture. But he had explained what light does to silver and had stumbled on a way to stop it, two clues that later inventors would need.

sections.heading: Tom Wedgwood's Shadow Pictures
paragraphs: The first person we know of who seriously tried to use light-sensitive silver to make pictures was a young Englishman named Thomas Wedgwood, usually called Tom. He was born in 1771, the son of Josiah Wedgwood, the famous potter whose factory made elegant plates, vases and cups that are still collected today. The Wedgwood family was rich, clever and interested in science. They were friends with many of the leading thinkers of the age, and Tom's sister Susannah later became the mother of Charles Darwin, which made Tom one of Darwin's uncles.

Tom Wedgwood was bright but often ill, and he never had a regular job. Instead he spent his time and his inheritance on ideas. He was a generous supporter of writers; in 1798 he and his brother gave the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge an allowance of money so he could write instead of becoming a preacher. Tom's own passion was the question of how we see. Growing up around a pottery business, he would have known that artists were constantly copying images onto ceramics, and that the camera obscura was used as a drawing aid. Could light do the copying itself?

Around 1800 he began experimenting. He soaked sheets of white paper and white leather in silver nitrate, a silver compound that dissolves in water. Then he laid objects on top, such as leaves, the wings of insects or pieces of lace, and put them in the sunshine. Where the object blocked the light, the paper stayed white. Where the Sun shone straight on the paper, it darkened. When he lifted the object off, there was a white silhouette on a dark background: a shadow picture.

He found that white leather worked even better than paper, darkening faster. He also tried copying pictures painted on glass. Light passed through the clear parts of the glass painting and darkened the paper underneath, while the painted parts blocked it, so the paper recorded a reversed copy. This is called contact printing, and photographers used the same basic idea for more than a hundred years.

Notice something important about these pictures. Light areas in the original came out dark, and dark areas came out light. Wedgwood's shadow pictures were what we would now call negatives. That was not a big problem for a silhouette of a leaf, but it would matter a great deal later.

Wedgwood's biggest dream was to capture the image inside a camera obscura. He tried, and failed. The picture formed by the camera's lens was far dimmer than direct sunlight, and his silver nitrate paper was not sensitive enough. After a long time in the camera, he could get nothing at all, or only the faintest trace. Bright sunlight acting on paper for a few minutes was enough for a shadow picture, but a camera image was perhaps hundreds of times weaker.

sections.heading: Davy's Report: Pictures to Be Seen by Candlelight
paragraphs: Tom Wedgwood shared his experiments with a rising young scientist named Humphry Davy. Davy, born in 1778 in Penzance in Cornwall, was the son of a woodcarver and had started out as an apprentice to a surgeon and apothecary. He became famous very young for experiments with nitrous oxide, the gas nicknamed laughing gas, which he breathed himself to test its effects, and he noticed it might one day help with pain during surgery.

In 1801 Davy moved to London to work at the Royal Institution, a new organization set up to bring science to the public. He was a sensation. His lectures were full of flashes, bangs and dramatic demonstrations, and crowds of fashionable Londoners, including many women, who were shut out of universities at the time, packed the lecture theater to hear him. By 1802, aged just 23, he had become the Institution's full lecturer in chemistry.

In June 1802 Davy published a short paper in the very first issue of the Journals of the Royal Institution. Its long, old-fashioned title described it as an account of a method of copying paintings on glass, and of making profiles, by the agency of light upon nitrate of silver, invented by T. Wedgwood, with observations by H. Davy. A profile here meant a silhouette of a person's face, a popular kind of portrait at the time. This paper is often counted as the first published account of making images with light-sensitive chemicals.

The paper explained Wedgwood's methods and added some of Davy's own experiments. Davy found that silver chloride was more sensitive than silver nitrate. He also tried using a solar microscope, a device that used sunlight and a lens to project an enlarged image of something tiny, such as an insect, onto a screen. He managed to record these magnified images on prepared paper, though only when the paper was placed very close to the lens where the light was strongest. Some historians credit this as the first idea of photographic enlargement.

But the paper was also an honest report of failure. The camera obscura image, it admitted, was too faint to record in any reasonable time. And the pictures they did make could not be kept. Once a shadow picture was made, it had to be stored in the dark. It could be looked at only briefly, by the light of a candle or an oil lamp, which was too weak and too red to darken the silver much. Bring it out into daylight, even for a few minutes, and the white parts slowly darkened too, until the whole picture disappeared into an even brown-black.

Davy and Wedgwood tried washing the pictures and coating them with varnish, but nothing worked. Davy, busy with other research, moved on. He went on to discover the elements sodium and potassium using electricity, and later invented a safety lamp for coal miners. Tom Wedgwood, whose health was getting worse, died in 1805 at the age of 34. Neither man knew that the chemist Scheele had already found, in ammonia, a way to wash the unchanged silver salt away.

Did any of Wedgwood's pictures survive? For many years, people hoped so. In 2008 a faint photograph of a leaf was offered at auction, attributed to Wedgwood and described as possibly the oldest photograph in the world. The sale was withdrawn after doubts were raised, and later research by the photography historian Larry Schaaf suggested it was probably made around 1839 by a woman named Sarah Anne Bright. As far as anyone knows, all of Wedgwood's pictures faded away, just as he and Davy predicted.

sections.heading: The Fixing Problem
paragraphs: Wedgwood and Davy's paper made one problem crystal clear. Photography historians call it the fixing problem, and it is worth understanding, because it held up the invention of photography for decades.

Here is the trouble in simple terms. Imagine a sheet of paper coated all over with a light-sensitive silver salt. You place a leaf on it in the sunshine. Where light falls, the silver salt breaks down and leaves dark specks of silver. Under the leaf, the salt is untouched and stays white. So far, so good. You have a picture.

But the white areas are not really finished. They are still covered with fresh, unused silver salt, just waiting for light. The moment you take the paper out to look at it, daylight starts working on those white areas too. Slowly they darken, catching up with the rest of the paper. Soon there is no difference between the parts that were under the leaf and the parts that were not. The picture has not faded in the usual sense. It has drowned in darkness.

To fix the picture, you need to get rid of every bit of unused silver salt after the picture is made, while keeping the dark silver specks that form the image. Then there is nothing left that can react to light, and the picture stops changing. It becomes permanent. This is what photographers later called fixing, and the chemical that does it is called a fixer. You will meet the most famous fixer, nicknamed hypo, later in this story.

Why was this so hard? Silver salts like silver nitrate dissolve easily in water, but silver chloride does not. Ordinary washing removed some of the chemical, but not enough. Early experimenters needed a liquid that would dissolve the unused silver salt without also dissolving or damaging the tiny silver grains of the picture. They also needed to know what to look for, and the chemistry of the time was still young. Scheele's ammonia trick and, later, ordinary strong salt water would turn out to work partly, by making the leftover silver salt much less sensitive or carrying it away. But in 1802 nobody connected these clues.

There was a second problem, too: sensitivity. Paper soaked in silver nitrate needed bright direct sunlight to change quickly. The image inside a camera obscura is far dimmer, because only the light passing through the small lens opening reaches it. Inventors needed both a more sensitive material and a way to fix it. It would take two more decades before anyone managed the first, and nearly four before the whole puzzle was solved.

sections.heading: Machines for Drawing
paragraphs: While chemists struggled with silver, ordinary people still needed pictures. In the early 1800s there were no photographs in newspapers, no snapshots of family members and no pictures of faraway places except those drawn by hand. Travelers who wanted to remember a mountain or a ruin had to sketch it. Scientists who wanted to record a fossil or a flower under the microscope had to draw it. Anyone who could not draw well was stuck, and good artists were expensive.

Inventors therefore kept improving drawing aids. One of the most popular was the camera lucida, patented in 1806 by the English chemist and physicist William Hyde Wollaston. Wollaston, who also discovered the metals palladium and rhodium, made up the name to contrast with the camera obscura. Camera lucida means "lit room", because it worked in ordinary daylight.

Despite its name, the camera lucida is not a camera at all and does not project an image. It is a small glass prism with four carefully angled faces, mounted on a stand above a sheet of paper. The artist looks down past the edge of the prism. Half of the eye sees the scene in front, bounced through the prism by two reflections so that it is the right way up, and the other half sees the paper. The brain blends the two views, so the landscape seems to float on the paper like a ghostly overlay. The artist can then trace the main outlines with a pencil.

The camera lucida was light, small enough to carry on a journey and needed no darkened room. Artists, travelers and especially scientists used it. Naturalists and microscope users kept using versions of it to draw specimens well into the 1900s. But it was tricky to use. If you moved your head even slightly, the image slid across the paper. Some people found the double view confusing, and the device did not give you any shading or detail. It only helped you draw. One frustrated user of a camera lucida would play a very important part in the story of photography, as you will see.

Other gadgets competed too. There were physionotrace machines that helped trace the profile of a sitter's face and engrave small portraits. Silhouette artists cut profiles from black paper in minutes. Engravers and lithographers, who printed pictures from carved metal plates or specially treated stones, made copies of paintings for books and prints. Each of these methods showed how strong the demand was for accurate, affordable pictures. Whoever could make light draw a picture by itself, and keep it, would find an eager world waiting.

sections.heading: An Inventor in Burgundy
paragraphs: Now let us travel to the rolling countryside of Burgundy in eastern France, to meet the man who would finally make light leave a lasting mark. Joseph Niépce was born on 7 March 1765 in the town of Chalon-sur-Saône, where his father was a wealthy lawyer. While studying at a religious college in Angers, he took the name Nicéphore, which comes from Greek and means something like "bringer of victory".

His early life was full of adventure and upheaval. France was shaken by the Revolution, which began in 1789. Niépce joined the French revolutionary army in 1792 and served as an officer, but poor health forced him to leave. He then worked as a local administrator in the district of Nice, by the Mediterranean. In 1795 he resigned to devote himself to inventing with his older brother Claude, and by 1801 the brothers had returned to the family estate near Chalon, where they also grew beets and made sugar.

The Niépce brothers' first big invention was not a camera but an engine. They called it the Pyréolophore, from Greek words meaning roughly "fire", "wind" and "carrier". It was one of the earliest internal combustion engines, meaning the fuel burned inside the engine itself rather than in a separate boiler, as in a steam engine. A bellows blew air into a chamber, a small dose of fine, burnable powder was dropped in and lit by a glowing fuse, and the sudden puff of burning gas pushed water out of a pipe at the back of a boat, shoving the boat forward. At first the fuel was lycopodium powder, made from the dusty spores of a plant called clubmoss, which flashes into flame. Because it was expensive, the brothers switched to finely crushed coal dust mixed with a little resin.

In 1807 the engine pushed a boat weighing about 900 kilograms upstream on the River Saône at Chalon, with about a dozen bursts every minute. The brothers had presented their work to French scientists the year before, and on 20 July 1807 they received a ten-year patent signed by Napoleon Bonaparte. It was an astonishing machine for its time. But it never became a business. Claude eventually moved to England to promote the engine, and over the following years he spent much of the family fortune on failed schemes. Nicéphore, back in France, turned more and more to a different dream.

That dream grew partly from lithography, a new printing method invented in Germany in the 1790s, in which an image drawn with greasy crayon on a flat stone could be inked and printed many times. Lithography became a craze in France in the 1810s. Niépce was excited by it, but he could not draw well. So he wondered: could light draw the image onto the stone or plate for him?

By about 1816, working at his country house at Saint-Loup-de-Varennes near Chalon, Niépce was building small camera obscuras and putting paper coated with silver chloride inside them. Letters he wrote to his family that year describe his results. He did manage to capture views from his workroom window on paper. In one letter he describes pointing the camera at a birdhouse with the windows open and getting a faint image of the window frames. He called these camera pictures "points de vue", or viewpoints. It was a huge step: unlike Wedgwood, he had recorded an actual camera image.

But Niépce ran into the same wall as Wedgwood and Davy. His pictures were negatives: the bright sky came out dark and the dark buildings came out pale. He tried to think of ways to reverse them. Worse, he still could not fix them. When he brought the paper out to look at it, the unused silver chloride kept darkening, and the faint pictures slowly sank into darkness. None of these early paper images survives.

Many people would have given up. Niépce instead decided the problem might be the silver itself. Silver salts darkened in light, which was why his pictures came out as negatives, and they kept on darkening, which was why they would not last. What if he used a material that behaved the opposite way? He began testing all sorts of substances that react to sunlight. And he became more and more interested in one of the strangest: a sticky black tar, a natural asphalt dug from the ground near the Dead Sea, that did not darken in the Sun at all. Instead, where sunlight touched it, it slowly hardened.

deepDive: What happens chemically when silver salts darken? Silver chloride (AgCl) and silver nitrate (AgNO3) contain silver as positively charged ions. When a packet of light with enough energy strikes a silver chloride crystal, it frees an electron, which can join a silver ion and turn it into a neutral silver atom. Clusters of such atoms are so tiny that they scatter and absorb light, making the material look grey, purple or black rather than shiny. Scheele's 1777 prism experiment showed this reaction depends on color: violet light is effective and red light almost useless, which we now explain by photon energy, since violet photons carry nearly twice the energy of deep red ones. In 1801 Johann Wilhelm Ritter used the same darkening to detect invisible ultraviolet rays beyond the violet end of the spectrum. Historians argue about how close each pioneer came. Schulze is honored in Germany as a forerunner, but he never tried to form an image of a scene. Scheele effectively discovered both the action of light on silver and a partial fixer, ammonia, yet did not link them to picture-making. Wedgwood and Davy clearly aimed at pictures and published in 1802, so some call Wedgwood the first photographer, but none of his images survives and the 2008 leaf photogram once credited to him is now thought to date from about 1839. Niépce's 1816 silver chloride camera images were probably the first true camera photographs, but they were unfixed negatives that have long since vanished. There is also a dating debate: the Schulze experiment is often given as 1727, but the original publication was 1719, describing work from about 1717. Finally, note the size of the sensitivity problem. Direct summer sunlight is very roughly a hundred thousand lux, while the image on a camera obscura screen might be hundreds or thousands of times dimmer, which is why shadow pictures worked in minutes and camera pictures barely worked at all.
funFact: Tom Wedgwood, who made some of the first pictures with light-sensitive silver around 1800, was the uncle of Charles Darwin: his sister Susannah was Darwin's mother.
